subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 6 periods = 240 minutes
Total: 6 periods · 4h 0min

periods.section_ref: Let's Take a Look Around Us!
periods.textbook_anchor: Let's Take a Look Around Us! — Draw a picture of your classroom and label the things in it (p. 124)
materials: Blackboard or chart paper for class list

time_bands.activity: The teacher invites students to look slowly around the room, asking: what do you see? Students call out objects aloud while the teacher writes a growing list on the board — desk, window, mat, bulb, switch, bag, bottle. No evaluation yet; the goal is a rich, shared inventory.

Students open their notebooks and draw their classroom as they see it now (Textbook p. 124). They label every object they draw, using the board list for spelling help. The teacher circulates quietly, prompting students who have drawn only furniture: what is on the wall? what is on the floor? what is near the window?

Students scan their own drawings and, beside each label, write a guess: what is this made of? Wood? Metal? Glass? Plastic? Something else? The teacher models one example on the board — 'window frame — wood' — and then invites students to work independently. Students who finish early look for objects they did not draw and add them.

A brief whole-class share: the teacher asks which material appeared most in students' lists. Students raise hands to vote. The teacher closes by posing an open question for thought: where do you think the metal in this room came from before it became part of a desk?

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe a familiar environment systematically and record what they see through labelled drawing.
periods.section_context: Classroom objects — desk, window, mat, bulb, switch, bag, bottle; materials identified as wood, metal, glass, plastic.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Did everyone draw the same things, or did different people notice different objects?' This surfaces how observation is selective and sets up later classification work. Keep the drawing phase unhurried — resist the urge to move to labelling before students have put enough objects on the page.

periods.textbook_anchor: See-through Materials! — Collect objects of different materials and look at a light source through them, ordering from most to least see-through (p. 126)
materials: Opaque plastic bottle or metal cup
A candle or the classroom window as a light source
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 126 — illustration of objects held up to a light source

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the question Khushi asked when she saw a tree through the glass window: why can we see through some things and not others? Students predict which of the collected objects on the demonstration table they can see through clearly, partially, or not at all. Predictions are voiced aloud — no writing yet.

In pairs, students take the objects set out on their desks and hold each one between their eye and the classroom window or a candle (Textbook p. 126). They record their findings in three columns in their notebook — 'See through clearly', 'Partly see through', 'Cannot see through' — and place each object's name in the right column. The teacher circulates, asking: what do you notice about objects in the first column — do they share any quality? What about the last column?

The teacher introduces the three words: transparent, translucent, opaque. Students write these three words as headings and copy their sorted list under each. Together the class builds one agreed example for each term on the board. The teacher connects Khushi's glass window: which word fits it?

Students share one object they were uncertain about and explain what confused them. The teacher closes by asking: have you ever seen a curtain, a stained-glass window, or coloured plastic that let some light through but changed the colour of things behind it? Students share brief memories.

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify materials by a physical property using direct observation and then name each category.
periods.section_context: Transparent, translucent, and opaque classification; objects tested — clear glass or plastic bottle, opaque bottle or metal cup, wax or tracing paper, cloth, white paper; light source as testing tool.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Can something be a little transparent? Where would we put it?' This productively disrupts the expectation of clean categories and opens up the idea of a spectrum — which mirrors the textbook's ordering task. If the classroom has coloured glass or a tinted water bottle, bring it to the centre as a discussion object.

periods.activity_title: Grouping Objects by Material and Tracing Their Sources
periods.textbook_anchor: What is it made of? — Complete the table grouping objects by material and add your own examples, including a material not in Khushi's list (p. 128)
materials: A few classroom objects to handle — wooden ruler, metal spoon, glass bottle, plastic bottle

time_bands.activity: The teacher holds up the wooden ruler, metal spoon, glass bottle, and plastic bottle one at a time. For each, students say what it is made of and try to name where that material comes from — 'wood comes from trees', 'metal comes from the ground'. The teacher writes these source-to-material chains on the board as students speak.

Students open their textbooks to Textbook p. 128 and read Khushi's table together. They then copy and complete the third column in their notebooks, writing names of objects they have seen at home or school made from wood, metal, glass, and plastic. They also add one extra row for a material Khushi left out — the textbook suggests clay or rubber — and give examples for it. The teacher circulates, prompting: 'Can you think of something your grandparents used that was made of clay?'

Pairs share their extra-row choices with the class. The teacher facilitates a brief discussion: why do you think plastic has become so common now when your grandparents may not have had as much of it? Students share what elders at home have told them about older materials — clay pots, brass vessels, jute bags — and the teacher draws these into the material chains on the board.

Students look at the board chains and choose the one they find most surprising — a material whose source they had not thought about before. They write one sentence in their notebooks about it. The teacher closes with an open question: if the source material — say, a forest — disappeared, what would happen to the objects made from it?

periods.implied_lo: Students can group everyday objects by the material they are made of and trace each material back to a natural source.
periods.section_context: Material groups — wood, metal, glass, plastic, clay, rubber; natural sources — trees, ore in the earth, sand, rubber plants; objects — wooden ruler, metal spoon, glass bottle, plastic bottle, clay pots, brass vessels, jute bags.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: When students mention what elders use or used, ask: 'Why do you think that material was used then? Is the reason different now?' This draws out the intergenerational and cultural thread without labelling it separately — it stays inside the material-grouping conversation.

periods.activity_title: Odd Pairs — Matching Objects with Wrong Materials
periods.textbook_anchor: Does it Bend? — List five objects and pair each with an unsuitable material, explaining why that material will not work (p. 130)
materials: Objects of different materials on the desk — wooden block, plastic ruler, cloth strip, glass bottle, metal tin

time_bands.activity: The teacher holds a cloth strip and asks: could we make a table leg out of this? Students respond. Then: why not? Students explain — it is too soft, it bends, it cannot hold weight. The teacher introduces the words hard, rigid, soft, flexible with the objects on the desk, and students take turns bending or tapping each one to feel the difference. The teacher taps a metal spoon on the wooden block, then on the cloth, and students describe the sounds they hear — inventing their own sound words as the textbook invites.

Students open their notebooks and write the heading 'Odd Pairs' (Textbook p. 130). They list five objects and, beside each, write a material that would be a bad choice for making it — for example, a glass hammer or a cloth window frame. For each pair they write one or two sentences explaining why the material is unsuitable, using words like hard, soft, rigid, flexible, transparent, or opaque from earlier in the chapter. The teacher circulates, prompting: 'Would a metal cushion be comfortable? Why not?'

Students share their most inventive Odd Pair with the class. The class votes on which pairing is the most absurd and gives reasons. The teacher uses this playfully: 'So a chocolate spoon — bad idea, but why? What property is missing?' This keeps the discussion grounded in properties, not just silliness.
Students write one sentence in their notebooks: 'A material is chosen for an object because…' and complete it in their own words. These are read aloud by two or three volunteers as a closing summary.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain how the physical properties of a material — hardness, flexibility — determine its suitability for a specific use.
periods.section_context: Properties — hard, rigid, soft, flexible; objects tested by tapping and bending — wooden block, plastic ruler, cloth strip, glass bottle, metal tin; Odd Pairs writing task.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Open question for deeper thinking: 'Is there any material that is both flexible and strong? Where have you seen something like that?' Students may name ropes, belts, or rubber bands — this stretches the binary of hard/soft into a more nuanced picture without leaving the section's content.

periods.activity_title: Sorting Matter — Solid, Liquid, and Gas
periods.textbook_anchor: Does it Flow? — Sort given objects into solid, liquid, or gas, and identify at least three confusing cases (p. 132)
materials: Word cards (optional) — ink, stone, smoke, ice, steam, spoon, honey, bottle, bag, water
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 132 — sorting diagram with tray, bottle, and balloon

time_bands.activity: The teacher holds up the stone, water bottle, and plastic bag filled with air. For each: does this hold its own shape, does it take the shape of its container, or does it escape an open container? Students respond and the teacher writes the three defining questions on the board. The class agrees on the words solid, liquid, gas as labels for three behaviours.

Students open to Textbook p. 132 and read the list of objects: ink, a stone, smoke, ice, steam, a spoon, honey, a bottle, a bag, water. In their notebooks they draw three simple shapes — a tray, a bottle, a balloon — and write each object's name inside the correct shape. They then add objects of their own in each category. The teacher circulates, pausing at edge cases: 'Where did you put ice? What about honey — does it flow slowly or is it a solid?'

The class discusses the confusing cases together: sand (flows like a liquid but each grain is a solid), sponge (solid but squishes), clay (solid but changes shape when pressed). Students write at least three confusing objects in a special section of their notebook and attempt an explanation. The teacher asks: 'What would happen to sand in the balloon — would it stay or escape?'

Students share one confusing object and their reasoning. The teacher closes with a question the chapter itself raises: 'Air is a gas — where does air go when you open a balloon?' Students respond freely, and the teacher affirms that this kind of wondering is exactly what scientists do.

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify matter as solid, liquid, or gas using the defining property of whether it holds its own shape, and can identify materials that are genuinely ambiguous.
periods.section_context: Solids, liquids, gases; objects sorted — ink, stone, smoke, ice, steam, spoon, honey, bottle, bag, water; ambiguous cases — sand, sponge, clay.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Can something change from one state to another? When does water become ice, and when does ice become water?' Students have lived experience of this — let them lead. This plants the seed of change-of-state thinking without requiring it to be formalised in this unit.

periods.activity_title: Natural or Artificial? — Drawing and Reflecting
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Draw three natural and three artificial things (p. 134)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 133 — Khushi's drawing of the mango tree; Textbook p. 134 — reflect tasks

time_bands.activity: The teacher shows Textbook p. 133 — Khushi's drawing of the mango tree — and asks: is a mango tree natural or made by people? Students agree it is natural. Then: what about a plastic chair? A brick wall? A river? Students respond and the teacher builds two columns on the board — Natural and Artificial — filling them with students' suggestions. The teacher introduces the idea that natural things can be living (plants, animals) or non-living (rocks, water, air), while artificial things are always made by people.

Students open to Textbook p. 133 and read the task at the bottom of the page. In their notebooks they write five examples in each column — Natural and Artificial — going beyond the board list. The teacher circulates, asking about edge cases: 'Is a planted tree in a garden natural or artificial?' Students discuss briefly in pairs and decide.

Students turn to Textbook p. 134 and complete the Draw task — drawing three natural and three artificial things and labelling each. They also complete the Match task at the bottom of the page, matching transparent, translucent, and opaque to the three objects given — a lamp shade of paper, a plate, and a glass used in spectacles. The teacher circulates and asks the Discuss prompt quietly: 'How would you find out if a shiny spoon is really metal or just painted to look metallic?' Students think and share.

A brief closing circle: the teacher asks each student to say one natural thing and one artificial thing they will look for on their way home. Students share quickly around the room. The teacher closes with an open question: 'Everything artificial started as something natural — can you trace your pencil back to a natural source?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can distinguish natural from artificial things using the criterion of human-made versus occurring in nature, and represent examples through drawing and matching.
periods.section_context: Natural things — mango tree, rocks, water, air, plants, animals; artificial things — plastic chair, brick wall, clothes, shoes, tables; transparency matching — lamp shade of paper (translucent), plate (opaque), glass in spectacles (transparent).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Open question for the mango-season prompt: 'Khushi drew mangoes on the tree — when do mangoes ripen in your area? What does that tell us about when she made her drawing?' This grounds seasonal observation in local knowledge without requiring a single correct answer.

assessment_items.question_text: Priya drew her classroom and listed what each object is made of. She wrote 'wood' next to her desk. Which of the following best describes what she did?

options.label: A
options.text: She invented a new material for classroom furniture.

options.label: B
options.text: She measured the size of her desk and recorded the number.

options.label: C
options.text: She observed an object and identified the material it is made of.

options.label: D
options.text: She sorted her desk into the category of artificial materials.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. The item checks whether students understand that labelling a drawn object with its material is an act of observation and identification of a social component of the immediate environment.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Let's Take a Look Around Us!
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe a familiar environment systematically and record what they see through labelled drawing.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has not connected drawing-and-labelling to observation; confuses a recording task with invention.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student associates the desk task with measurement rather than material identification — a confusion between two types of recording.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student conflates identifying a material with the Natural–Artificial classification introduced later in the chapter.

assessment_items.question_text: Ravi holds a piece of wax paper up to the classroom window. He can see a dim shape of the window frame but cannot see it clearly. Which label fits the wax paper?

options.label: A
options.text: Flexible, because wax paper can be bent easily.

options.label: B
options.text: Opaque, because you cannot see a clear image through it.

options.label: C
options.text: Translucent, because light passes through it only partially.

options.label: D
options.text: Transparent, because some light passes through it.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. The item targets the boundary between transparent and translucent — the most commonly confused pair in the section.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify materials by a physical property using direct observation and then name each category.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with using the scientific method in investigations, as well as familiarity with other crosscutting concepts such as energy, matter, and systems that apply across the domains of science and engineering

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has overgeneralised: because some light passes through, they choose transparent, missing the key qualifier 'clearly'. They have not distinguished the degree of light transmission.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student focuses on the absence of a clear image rather than the presence of partial transmission — a partial reading of the opaque definition.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has confused a light-transmission property with a physical/mechanical property from a different section of the chapter.

assessment_items.question_text: Meena wants to add a new row to the material-grouping table in her notebook. She chooses clay as her extra material. Name two objects made of clay and say where clay comes from in nature.
expected_elements: Names at least two objects made of clay (e.g., pots, cups, tiles, figurines, lamps/diyas).
States that clay comes from the earth / soil / ground (any equivalent natural-source description is acceptable).
Response is specific to clay, not confused with another material.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any regionally familiar clay objects — in many parts of India, students may name diyas, surahis, or kulhads as readily as generic pots. Regionally varied answers are acceptable and correct. Full marks require both a source (earth/soil) and at least two objects.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can group everyday objects by the material they are made of and trace each material back to a natural source.

competency.competency_text: Describes usage of natural resources in their immediate environment

expected_elements: Names at least two objects made of clay (e.g., pots, cups, tiles, figurines, lamps/diyas).
States that clay comes from the earth / soil / ground (any equivalent natural-source description is acceptable).
Response is specific to clay, not confused with another material.

assessment_items.question_text: Arjun writes this Odd Pair: 'A rubber window frame — rubber is too soft and flexible, so it will not hold the glass in place.' Is Arjun's explanation correct? Write whether you agree or disagree and give one property-based reason for your answer.
expected_elements: Student agrees with Arjun (the explanation is correct).
Student uses at least one property word — soft, flexible, rigid, hard — to support the agreement.
Student's reason connects the property to the function of holding glass (i.e., a window frame must be rigid/hard).
assessment_items.annotation: The expected answer is agreement with Arjun. A student who disagrees but gives a coherent property-based argument (very unusual) may receive partial credit at the teacher's discretion. The key assessment target is the use of a property word to justify a material-suitability claim.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how the physical properties of a material — hardness, flexibility — determine its suitability for a specific use.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: Student agrees with Arjun (the explanation is correct).
Student uses at least one property word — soft, flexible, rigid, hard — to support the agreement.
Student's reason connects the property to the function of holding glass (i.e., a window frame must be rigid/hard).

assessment_items.question_text: A student pours honey slowly from a jar. It spreads across the plate and takes the plate's shape. What does this tell us about honey?

options.label: A
options.text: Honey is a gas because it moves.

options.label: B
options.text: Honey is a liquid because it flows and takes the shape of its container.

options.label: C
options.text: Honey is a solid because it does not look like water.

options.label: D
options.text: Honey is a solid because it is thick and heavy.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is C. Honey is a classic ambiguous case from the sorting activity. The item tests whether students apply the defining criterion — flows and takes the shape of a container — rather than relying on appearance or texture.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify matter as solid, liquid, or gas using the defining property of whether it holds its own shape, and can identify materials that are genuinely ambiguous.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with disciplinary core ideas in the natural sciences, as well as in engineering, technology, and applications of science, which reflect the content that will be learned across subject areas in later Grades

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student is using texture or density (thick, heavy) as the defining property rather than shape-behaviour — a common misconception about viscous liquids.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has over-applied the idea that 'moving = gas', confusing movement with the gas-specific property of escaping open containers.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student is using visual appearance (does not look like water) as the classification criterion rather than the scientific property of shape-holding.

assessment_items.task: Draw three natural things and three artificial things from your own neighbourhood. Label each drawing with its name and write one word beside it that tells you whether it is natural or artificial. Then match these three words to one example each from your drawings: Transparent — Translucent — Opaque.
assessment_items.scaffold: Box 1 — My three NATURAL things (draw and label each): [space] | Box 2 — My three ARTIFICIAL things (draw and label each): [space] | Box 3 — Match the word to one of your drawings or to any object you know: Transparent → _______ | Translucent → _______ | Opaque → _______
format_of_output: Three labelled drawings of natural things
Three labelled drawings of artificial things
Three filled-in matches connecting transparency terms to examples
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any natural things found in the student's own region — a coconut tree, a river, a paddy field, a goat are all correct. Regionally varied answers are acceptable and correct for the natural-things section. For the transparency matching, the correct pairing from the textbook is: Transparent — glass in spectacles; Translucent — lamp shade made of paper; Opaque — plate. Accept equivalent examples from the student's drawings if the property rationale is sound.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can distinguish natural from artificial things using the criterion of human-made versus occurring in nature, and represent examples through drawing and matching.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The task shows whether the student can apply the natural/artificial criterion to objects from their own context and simultaneously recall the transparency classification from earlier in the chapter — two connected ideas presented through drawing and labelling.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Box 1 and Box 2 assess the natural/artificial distinction; Box 3 assesses retention and application of the transparent/translucent/opaque categories. A student who completes all three boxes correctly has demonstrated integration across the chapter's two main property threads.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: drawings are clearly labelled; the natural/artificial label is correct for each; all three transparency terms are matched to a plausible object with no cross-contamination (e.g., not calling a plate transparent). Weak: natural and artificial labels are mixed up or absent; transparency terms are guessed randomly or two terms are assigned to the same category.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may write names and one describing word instead of drawing. Students who name regional natural objects (local trees, rivers, animals) should receive full credit — the task is not limited to textbook examples.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Drawing with labels and a written matching task
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Drawing allows students who are still developing written fluency to demonstrate conceptual understanding; the matching task provides a written anchor that the teacher can quickly scan for accuracy of the transparency terminology.
